content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the edible seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to tropical regions of Asia, Africa and South America. They have a delicate buttery‑nutty flavor, slightly sweet, and a soft crunchy texture. Cashews are sold raw, roasted, and lightly salted.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cashews belong to the sumac family and are more closely related to mango than to most other nuts.
The seed grows outside the true nut, attached to a fleshy pseudofruit called the cashew apple.
Only the apple’s shell contains toxic urushiol, which is removed before the nuts are sold.
Cashews are commonly used to make nut butter, oil, and vegan cheese alternatives.
In India, cashews are traditionally featured in festive dishes and sweets.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fats help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contains copper and magnesium
items.content: Copper supports collagen formation, while magnesium aids muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Cashews provide protein useful for tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine (B1), pyridoxine (B6) and folate contribute to energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Vitamin E and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashews can trigger allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Because of their energy density, portion control is recommended.

items.title: Toxic raw cashew apple
items.content: The raw fruit contains urushiol, a toxin that must be removed during processing.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Cashews contain oxalates, so people prone to kidney stones should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, or processed into cashew butter and oil. Lightly salted cashews are a great option for appetizers and Asian‑style dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: An empanada is a small, closed pastry traditionally filled with sweet or savory fillings. In this case it refers to a fruit empanada, where pieces of ripe fruit such as apples, pears or berries are wrapped in dough with sugar and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Empanadas originate from Latin America, but variations exist in many world cuisines.
Fruit empanadas are often served hot so the crust stays crisp and the filling aromatic.
The dough is usually made from wheat flour, butter and a touch of sugar, giving it a light sweetness.
In some regions the filling is spiced with cinnamon and nutmeg.
Empanadas are portable – they are compact and require no additional utensils.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The fruit filling provides vitamin C, vitamin A and various antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fruit contributes dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The pastry uses a modest amount of butter, resulting in lower saturated fat compared with many baked goods.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Combined carbohydrates from fruit and a small amount of fat make empanadas a quick source of energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour dough can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The fruit filling is often sweetened, so those monitoring blood sugar should consume empanadas in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite a relatively light crust, empanadas can be calorie‑dense due to butter and sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Empanadas can be enjoyed warm or at room temperature. Cut them in half to reveal the fragrant filling. Serve with a light yogurt dip or dust with powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store empanadas in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage keep them refrigerated – up to 5 days, or freeze in a zip‑lock bag where they retain flavor for up to 3 months.

ice-cream-cone-soft-serve-chocolate-waff.title: Ice cream cone, soft serve, chocolate, waffle cone

content.title: About
content.content: Soft‑serve chocolate ice cream served in a crisp waffle cone. The combination of creamy texture and rich chocolate flavor makes it a popular treat in cafés and on the street.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate soft‑serve is commonly served in waffle cones in the US and Europe.
The waffle cone adds a crunchy texture and a subtle toasted flavor.
Traditional recipes use milk, cream, sugar and cocoa mass.
Soft‑serve is frozen at a higher temperature than regular ice cream, giving it a lighter, airy consistency.
Waffle cones can be tinted and decorated with sprinkles.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Dairy ingredients provide calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa mass is rich in flavonoids that may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Provides quick energy from sugars and fats.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream contain vitamins B2 and B12, important for metabolism.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Sweet chocolate flavor can stimulate serotonin production, improving mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dairy components can cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to casein.

items.title: Potential nut or soy additives
items.content: Some recipes may include nut‑based or soy‑based emulsifiers.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The waffle cone adds extra calories and carbohydrates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve immediately after preparation while the ice cream is still soft. Top with sprinkles, nuts, fruit sauce, or caramel for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. The waffle cone is best used right away, as it can become soggy over time.
